The resolution source for this market will be information from the Hong Kong Observatory, specifically the "Absolute Daily Max (deg. C)" the specified date once information is finalized in the relevant "Daily Extract", available here: https://www.weather.gov.hk/en/cis/climat.htm

This market can not resolve until data for this date has been published.

The resolution source for this market measures temperatures in Celsius to one decimal place (eg, 9.1°C). Thus, this is the level of precision that will be used when resolving the market.

Any revisions to temperatures recorded after data is initially published for this market's timeframe will not be considered for this market's resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description: Persistent showers and thunderstorms driven by a broad trough of low pressure over the South China Sea are suppressing solar heating and convective development, anchoring Hong Kong's August 1 daytime maximum near 28°C per official Hong Kong Observatory guidance. This aligns with current model consensus showing extensive cloud cover and heavy precipitation that limits surface warming, in contrast to typical August climatology of 31–32°C highs under clearer subtropical conditions. A rapid clearing of cloud cover or delayed onset of rain could allow greater insolation and push temperatures higher, though current observations indicate low probability of such shifts before resolution.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Persistent showers and thunderstorms from a broad trough of low pressure over the South China Sea are capping daytime heating in Hong Kong on August 2, 2026, aligning trader consensus with highs near 26–27°C.** 

Official Hong Kong Observatory guidance forecasts a maximum of 28°C under mainly cloudy skies with heavy showers and squally thunderstorms at times, high humidity (80–95%), and south winds. These conditions reduce solar radiation and promote evaporative cooling, keeping temperatures well below the seasonal August average of around 31–32°C. Multi-model consensus and current observations on August 1 reinforce this pattern, with similar suppression already evident. The trough is projected to weaken later in the week, but unsettled weather persists through August 2, limiting upside risk to 29°C or higher. This meteorological setup drives the market-implied probabilities, with 27°C at 42% and 26°C at 32% reflecting the most likely range under prevailing cloud, rain, and humidity.

eventMetadata.context_description: Current forecasts from European models show Milan’s August 3 maximum temperature clustering near 35–36 °C amid a lingering heat dome driven by a strong subtropical anticyclone and advection of hot, dry African air masses. Clear skies and strong solar insolation under subsiding air favor daytime heating, while the urban heat-island effect in the Po Valley adds 1–2 °C locally. The close 38.5 %–34.5 % split between the 35 °C and 36 °C outcomes reflects minor model spread in the timing of any weak northwesterly flow or thin high cloud that could trim the peak by 1 °C, together with typical uncertainty in the precise hour of maximum temperature. Earlier heatwave peaks on August 2 support elevated baselines, yet ensemble guidance has not shifted decisively above 36 °C for the 3rd.

eventMetadata.context_description: **Trader sentiment for Kuala Lumpur's August 3 daily maximum temperature centers on short-range forecast guidance projecting highs of 32–34 °C amid typical southwest monsoon conditions.** Regional models show modest day-to-day variability driven by afternoon convective cloud build-up and scattered showers, which can trim peak readings by 1–2 °C when widespread, or allow clearer skies to push temperatures toward the upper end of the range. High humidity (often 70–80 %) and the urban heat-island effect in the Klang Valley sustain elevated baseline readings near the seasonal norm of 31–32 °C, while light winds limit mixing. With 33 °C and 34 °C outcomes separated by just four percentage points, small shifts in the next 48-hour model runs—particularly updates on timing of convective initiation—will likely determine the final measured maximum at official stations.
